other_words: Writing this on the train at 7am and I could murder a coffee. I'm a partner in a litigation team and we're three weeks into a trial that is frankly killing me. What I actually want to look at is how I am with my team. I'm very good at what I do, and I know it. The problem is I've started to think nobody else is. Last Tuesday a senior associate redrafted a witness statement, and I rewrote the entire thing at midnight rather than explain what was wrong, then told her in front of the others that I'd 'fixed it'. I saw her face. I didn't apologise. When the client thanked the associates on the call rather than me, I was irritated for the rest of the day, and I made sure my name went first on the next email thread. I tell myself standards matter, and they do, but if I'm honest, part of it is that I need to be the one who's right in the room. When someone challenges me in a meeting I can feel myself go cold, and I'll hold it against them for weeks. Two juniors have asked to move to another partner this year. The commute is murder and home is quiet now the kids are at university, so work is most of who I am.

insights.text: You wrote "i want to go straight back to it"; the texts describe this as wanting a pleasure again, or the means to it, because it is remembered.

Your words “i want to go straight back to it” fit only loosely what the Vedic and yogic texts call Rāga (attachment). Rāga is what follows upon pleasure (YS 2.7). Vyāsa: in one who has known pleasure, preceded by the memory of pleasure, the greed, thirst and craving (gardha, tṛṣṇā, lobha) for pleasure or for its means — that is rāga.

Read through the Jain texts, your words “i want to go straight back to it” come closest to what they call Lobha (greed) (a partial match for Rāga (attachment)). Conduct-deluding karma includes the sixteen passions: anger, pride, deceit and greed, each in four grades named endless-binding (anantānubandhī), non-renunciation (apratyākhyāna), renunciation (pratyākhyāna) and smouldering (saṃjvalana) (TS 8.9, Digambara recension).

Read through the Buddhist texts, your words “i want to go straight back to it” come closest to what they call Kāmacchanda (sensual desire) (a partial match for Rāga (attachment)). Contemplating dhammas as the five hindrances: when sensual desire is present in him the monk knows 'there is sensual desire in me'; when absent, 'there is no sensual desire in me'; he knows how the unarisen sensual desire arises, how the arisen sensual desire is abandoned, and how the abandoned sensual desire does not arise again.

YS: attachment rests on pleasure (YS 2.7); Vyāsa glosses it as greed, thirst and covetousness (gardha, tṛṣṇā, lobha) for the pleasure or its means, preceded by the memory of pleasure (YB 2.7). Gītā: from dwelling on objects comes attachment, from attachment desire (BhG 2.62); desire-anger is 'the enemy here' (BhG 3.37). Suttas: sensual desire (kāmacchanda) is known as present or absent, as arising and as abandoned (MN 10:36; DN 22:13); craving (taṇhā) that delights here and there is the origin of suffering, and its fading away is cessation (DN 22:19–20). TS: greed (lobha) is one of the four passions (TS 8.9), because of which the soul takes in karmic matter (TS 8.2). Under the one-truth principle, they describe it from different standpoints: the match is a partial match, not an identity.

Rāga is not kāmacchanda, and neither is lobha. (1) Framework: YS rāga is one of five kleśas growing in the field of avidyā (YS 2.4). The Gītā's kāma is born of the guṇa rajas and is one enemy with anger (BhG 3.37). Kāmacchanda is a hindrance: a state to be noticed and abandoned in meditation (MN 10:36). Taṇhā is the origin of suffering (DN 22:19). Jain lobha is a passion-felt deluding karma (kaṣāya-vedanīya, TS 8.9) and a literal cause of karmic matter binding the soul (TS 8.2). (2) Scope: YS rāga covers any remembered pleasure and its means (YB 2.7). Kāmacchanda is sensual desire. Taṇhā in DN 22 also includes craving for being and for non-being (DN 22:19); the Yoga puts the wish to go on being under a different kleśa (abhiniveśa, YS 2.9). Jain lobha comes in four intensities, anantānubandhī to saṃjvalana (TS 8.9), a grading no other lens uses. The Theravāda lists grade it differently, by depth: a hindrance that keeps jhāna from arising (Vism IV), greed as a root of unwholesome consciousness (Vism XIV), and sensual lust as one of the five lower fetters (Vism XXII). (3) What is freed: the Yoga ends in the seer's aloneness (YS 2.25), the suttas in the cessation of craving (DN 22:20), the Jain path in the soul's release from karmic matter (TS 8.2). The self-question behind these three ends is not yet reconciled (row ot:provisional-self-question in one_truth.json).
You wrote “i want to go straight back to it”. The texts pair what they call Rāga (attachment) with this practice.

insights.text: You wrote "What I actually want to look at is how I am with my team"; the texts describe this as holding oneself high, wanting to be displayed (vism xiv).

Read through the Vedic and yogic texts, your words “What I actually want to look at is how I am with my team” come closest to what they call Āsurī sampad (the demonic endowment) (a partial match for Māna (conceit)). Hypocrisy, arrogance, conceit, anger, harshness and ignorance belong to one born to the demonic endowment (BhG 16.4); it leads to bondage (16.5).

Your words “What I actually want to look at is how I am with my team” fit only loosely what the Buddhist texts call Māna (conceit). Vism XXII: the fetters are ten states, beginning with lust for form, so called because they bind aggregates to aggregates, action to its fruit, and beings to suffering. Lust for form, lust for the formless, conceit, restlessness and ignorance are the five higher fetters; personality view, doubt, adherence to rules and observances, sensual lust and resentment are the five lower fetters.

Each names a false or inflated 'I'. YS: I-am-ness is the seeming identity of the power of the seer and the power of seeing (YS 2.6). Vyāsa: the puruṣa is the seer's power, the buddhi the power of seeing (YB 2.6). Gītā: arrogance and conceit (darpa, abhimāna) belong to the demonic endowment (BhG 16.4), which leads to bondage (BhG 16.5). TS: pride (māna) is one of the four passions (TS 8.9), by which the soul takes in karmic matter (TS 8.2). Visuddhimagga: personality view (sakkāyadiṭṭhi) regards form and the other aggregates as self (Vism XVII) and is one of the five lower fetters; conceit (māna) is a defilement and a fetter that remains until the arahat path (Vism XXII). Under the one-truth principle, they describe it from different standpoints: the match is a partial match, not an identity.

On the sense of 'I': Jain, Yoga, Upaniṣadic and Buddhist texts all teach that one is not the body, nor any passing state of mind. The Yoga Sūtra calls the seer's seeming oneness with the mind 'I-am-ness'; Theravāda texts teach seeing 'this is not mine, I am not this'. They differ on what is left: Jain texts, many souls whose changing states are their own; the Yoga Sūtra, many seers that never change; the Upaniṣads, a self that is brahman; Theravāda texts, nothing that is a self. These are different answers, not one.

Asmitā is not pride. YS 2.6 names a confusion of the seer with its instrument, a structural error that is present even without any haughtiness. The Gītā's darpa and abhimāna and the Jain māna are attitudes of self-exaltation: the Gītā lists them among the marks of a bad endowment (BhG 16.4), and TS grades māna in four intensities (TS 8.9). They meet only in the 'I'. Personality view comes closest to asmitā, since both take something that is not the self as the self. The Yoga also counts that as an error (YS 2.5), but it corrects the error by isolating a real seer (YS 2.25). The Visuddhimagga's remedy is to abandon the view, which is one of the five lower fetters, and conceit remains until the arahat path (Vism XXII). It does not isolate a seer in the view's place. Whether a seer remains is not yet reconciled (row ot:provisional-self-question of one_truth.json).
